item.title: Comment on It’s happening at The New York Times by Blackthorne
item.description:
Reply to Der Zeit:

The Times as a news source was lost long ago to first contact with AI and the need to conform to the imperatives of the dopamine/attention economy. It’s 85% recipes and word games and lifestyle and coffee grinder reviews and identity and diet and exercise routines. The information density is LOW. Will generative AI change that? (Especially as it becomes ubiquitous?) Doubtful.

The information density is low perhaps if you read every single thing on the NYT website, but cooking/games/wirecutter aren't published at the expense of the higher information density articles. If anything these sections subsidize the higher information density articles. The fluff sections are also the sections where generative AI is likely to be more effective, so if anything it should free up resources for the journalistic arm of the NYT

item.title: Comment on Kevin Kelly’s fifty travel tips by mento
item.description:
Reply to Tyler:

"Crash a wedding. You are not a nuisance; you are the celebrity guest! The easiest way to do this is to find the local wedding hall where weddings happen on schedule and approach a wedding party with a request to attend. They will usually feel honored. You can offer the newlyweds a small token gift of cash if you want. You will be obliged to dance. Take photos of them; they will take photos of you. It will make your day and theirs. (I’ve crashed a wedding in most of the countries I have visited.)"

This may work in Azerbaijan, but certainly not in any developed country I've ever visited.

"The most significant criteria to use when selecting travel companions is: do they complain or not, even when complaints are justified? No complaining! Complaints are for the debriefing afterwards when travel is over."

Do not travel with my children, got it.

"Large-scale luxury cruises have no appeal to me, yet a small boat cruise is an entirely different species and a valid option worth considering. The advantage of a cruise is that your hotel travels with you, so you unpack only once. It is especially useful for small groups because it eliminates the eternal negotiation of deciding where to eat. (You always eat on the boat.) The advantages of a small boat cruise over a huge boat are several: you disembark very quickly, very often, at smaller more intimate places than large boats can do. And the options for activities are more active than just shopping: such as snorkeling, kayaking, bicycling, hiking, visiting local families and communities. Overall you spend far more time doing things off the boat than on. I define a small boat as 40 passengers or fewer. The per day cost is high, but almost every minute of it is quality time, unlike a series of bus rides. Examples of places I’ve loved a small boat cruise; The Galapagos, Alaska inland passageway, Mekong River, Coast of Turkey, and Kerala, India."

Yes I love being seasick on small boats for extended periods of time.

There is some okay stuff in this list but overall it's for a very specific type of travel beyond just "engagement and experience", which I find often happens in places where I have enough in common with someone (language, for one) to have a deeper conversation. A bit different from a local telling you in pidgin English why they think Trump/Obama/whoever "very good!".

I don’t think I want to follow any of this guy’s advice, he is trying too hard to be unconventional. Maybe that’s what happens when you’ve visited every country 50 times.

He could have also said “ make sure you get arrested for some petty offence , the conversations you will have with your cellmates will be invaluable , and a window into the soul of the country. On your way out thanks the guards for their hospitality “
